title: Which Way Round? P(A|B) vs P(B|A)

steps.body:
The same 40 students sit in the crossing cell. But *what you are told* decides what you divide by.

Told they take the bus → divide by the bus row: 40/100.
Told they play a sport → divide by the sport column: 40/110.

Same numerator, different denominator, different answer. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are **not** the same number.
You are told the student takes the bus. Change the condition to see why “given” selects a row or column as the new denominator.

widget.prompt: Compare both directions. Choose the condition named by “given,” then choose the joint cell that becomes the numerator.
widget.successFeedback: Given bus makes the 100-person bus row the denominator; the 40-person bus-and-sport intersection is the numerator, so 40/100 = 0.400.
widget.explorationFeedback: Switch between at least two candidate conditions so you can compare how the same joint cell produces different denominators.
widget.conditionFeedback: The phrase “given they take the bus” restricts the world to the bus row, not the sport column or the whole table.
widget.cellFeedback: Inside the bus row, select the intersection that also satisfies “plays a sport”: the 40-person cell.

predict.prompt: The same 40 students are in both P(sport | bus) and P(bus | sport). What changes when the condition reverses?

options.label: Both probabilities must stay the same

predict.reveal: The intersection can remain the same 40 students, but “given bus” uses the 100 bus riders while “given sport” uses the 110 sport players. Reversing a conditional changes the reference group.

cml.actionGoal: Change the conditioned row or column and coordinate its total with the joint-cell numerator.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Keep the joint count 40 fixed but double the sport-only count among walkers. Which reversed conditional changes, and why?

explanation.prompt: Why does the word “given” determine the denominator?

options.label: It restricts the sample space to the group named after “given,” so that group total becomes the denominator.
options.feedback: Exactly. Conditional probability measures a part inside the restricted reference group.

options.label: Every probability from a two-way table must divide by the grand total.
options.feedback: The grand total is used only before conditioning. “Given” replaces it with the selected row or column total.

explanationVariants: The bus row holds 100 students and 40 of them play a sport: 40/100 = 0.40.

widget.prompt: P(plays a sport | takes the bus). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the joint probability 40/200 — dividing by everyone. The condition already cut the world down to the 100 bus riders.
That is 40/110, which conditions on **sport** instead. You were told the travel method, so the sport column is not the surviving world.
That is P(sport) for the whole school. The point of conditioning is that the bus riders need not match the school average.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Of the 100 bus riders, 40 play a sport: 0.40.

steps.body: Now flip what you are told.
explanationVariants: The sport column holds 110 students and 40 of them take the bus: 40/110 ≈ 0.364.
P(bus | sport) = 0.20/0.55 ≈ 0.364. Same 0.20 on top as before — only the denominator changed.

widget.prompt: P(takes the bus | plays a sport). Give a decimal, to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 40/100 = P(sport | bus) — the reverse conditional. Here you are told the sport, so you divide by the 110 who play, not the 100 who ride.
That is the joint 40/200. A conditional divides by its condition, and the condition here contains 110 students.
That is P(bus) across the whole school. Being told the student plays a sport should move that number — it lands at 40/110 ≈ 0.364.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Of the 110 who play a sport, 40 take the bus: 40/110 ≈ 0.364.

steps.body:
Swapping the two sides is the most expensive mistake in probability.

*Almost every flu patient has a cough* does **not** mean *almost every cougher has flu*. The first divides by the flu patients; the second divides by the far larger crowd of coughers.

When a claim conditions on something, ask: **which group is underneath?**

explanationVariants: "Of the students who walk, 70% play a sport" divides by the walkers — that is P(sport | walks) = 70/100.
The group named after "of the" is the condition. Everything else is the event being measured inside it.

widget.prompt: "Of the students who walk, 70% play a sport." Which probability is that?

options.label: P(plays a sport | walks) = 70/100
options.feedback: Right — the walkers are the group being divided by, so they sit under the line.

options.label: P(walks | plays a sport) = 70/110
options.feedback: That reverses the sentence. It would read "of the students who play a sport, 64% walk" — a true statement, but a different one.

options.label: P(walks and plays a sport) = 70/200
options.feedback: That is the joint probability, 0.35 — the share of the *whole school*. The sentence restricts attention to walkers first.

options.label: P(walks) = 100/200
options.feedback: That is the condition on its own. The 70% describes what happens *inside* that group.

steps.body: Match each phrasing to its fraction.
explanationVariants: The condition sets the denominator: bus → 100, sport → 110, everyone → 200.
All three fractions share the numerator 40. Only the group underneath changes.

widget.prompt: Each statement uses the same 40 students. Match it to its fraction.

left.label: Given they take the bus, they play a sport
Given they play a sport, they take the bus
They take the bus and play a sport

pairErrors.feedback: Being told they ride the bus makes the 100 bus riders the world, so the denominator is 100, not 110.
An "and" statement conditions on nothing — its denominator is everybody: 200.

widget.missFeedback: Find the word "given". Whatever follows it is the denominator; with no "given", the denominator is all 200.
widget.successFeedback: Three statements, one numerator, three denominators — that is the whole idea of conditioning.

hints: The condition is "plays no sport". Find how many students that is, and use it as the denominator.
The no-sport column holds 60 + 30 = 90 students. Now count the walkers inside that column.
30 of those 90 walk. Divide, and round to three places.
explanationVariants: The no-sport column has 90 students, and 30 of them walk: 30/90 ≈ 0.333.
P(walks | no sport) = P(walks and no sport)/P(no sport) = 0.15/0.45 ≈ 0.333.

widget.prompt: P(walks | plays no sport). Give a decimal, to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30/100 = P(no sport | walks) — the reversed conditional. You were told about sport, so the 90 non-players are the denominator, not the 100 walkers.
That is the joint 30/200. Conditioning on "no sport" shrinks the world to 90 students, so the denominator cannot still be 200.
That is P(no sport) = 90/200, the condition itself. The question asks what fraction of that group walks.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The no-sport column holds 90 students, 30 of whom walk: 30/90 ≈ 0.333.

takeaways: P(A | B) and P(B | A) share a numerator but divide by different groups — they are almost never equal.
The condition is the denominator. Find it before you compute anything.
"Of the X, some fraction are Y" means P(Y | X). Reversing it reverses the meaning.
steps.teaser: Next: rearrange the conditional formula and you get a rule for AND.

concept.body: The bar in P(A | B) is not symmetric. Whatever stands to the **right** of the bar is the group you are standing inside; whatever stands to the left is what you are counting there. Swap them and you have changed the question.

explanationVariants: In P(sport | bus), the bus riders are the world: 100 of them.
The condition follows the bar, and the condition always becomes the denominator.

widget.prompt: In P(plays a sport | takes the bus), which number goes on the bottom?

options.label: 100 — the bus riders
options.feedback: Right — the condition is on the right of the bar, and the condition is what you divide by.

options.label: 110 — the sport players
options.feedback: That would be the denominator for P(bus | sport). Here the bus is the condition, so its 100 goes underneath.

options.label: 200 — everyone
options.feedback: That denominator belongs to joint probabilities, which condition on nothing. The bar means the world has already shrunk.
